subsystems.name: Propulsion
subsystems.role: makes thrust; modern launchers use staged-combustion or full-flow engines burning kerosene, methane or hydrogen.

subsystems.name: Airframe and tanks
subsystems.role: holds cryogenic propellant while staying light enough to reach orbit.
parts: aluminium-lithium or stainless steel tank barrels

subsystems.name: Recovery system
subsystems.role: brings the booster back so it can fly again.

subsystems.name: Avionics and flight software
subsystems.role: flies the ascent, the landing and the payload deployment.

subsystems.name: Spacecraft bus
subsystems.role: the modular platform that carries the payload once in orbit.

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: gets the vehicle to the pad, tested and tracked.

buildSteps.title: Design and simulate
buildSteps.detail: Engineers size the tanks and engines against a target orbit, then run thousands of simulated flights to tune the guidance.

buildSteps.title: Form the tanks
buildSteps.detail: Aluminium-lithium panels are joined by friction stir welding, or stainless steel rings are welded into barrels; lighter tanks mean more payload.

buildSteps.title: Build and test engines
buildSteps.detail: Turbopumps, injectors and chambers are machined — often 3D-printed in one piece — then fired repeatedly on test stands to prove they survive throttling and restart.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the stages
buildSteps.detail: Tanks, engines, plumbing and avionics are stacked and the whole stage is pressure- and leak-tested.

buildSteps.title: Static fire
buildSteps.detail: The stacked rocket fires its engines held down on the pad, checking thrust, software and sensors before launch.

buildSteps.title: Launch and stage separation
buildSteps.detail: The first stage burns for a few minutes, separates, and the upper stage finishes the job of reaching orbital velocity.

buildSteps.title: Recover the booster
buildSteps.detail: After separation the first stage flips, coasts, re-enters, steers with grid fins, and relights engines to land on a ship or at the pad.

buildSteps.title: Refurbish and refly
buildSteps.detail: The booster is inspected, engines cleaned and components replaced as needed, then flown again — the core of the cost saving.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and commission
buildSteps.detail: The payload separates, solar arrays unfurl, and the satellite or crewed vehicle is checked out and handed over to its operator.

prerequisites.tech: Cryogenic rocket engines and propellant handling
prerequisites.why: liquid oxygen with kerosene, methane or hydrogen is the only practical way to get useful mass to orbit.
a booster only survives re-entry if it can steer and kill its velocity to within metres.
heat shields that survive repeated re-entry are still the hardest part of full reuse.
high-efficiency thrusters make small satellites and long-life spacecraft practical.
reuse only pays off if vehicles can be built and turned around quickly.

pathway.milestone: reusable first stages flying many missions each
pathway.unlocks: routine, much cheaper access to low Earth orbit and large satellite constellations.

pathway.milestone: fully reusable two-stage vehicles and higher launch cadence
pathway.unlocks: costs closer to the price of propellant, and much larger payloads.
deep-space missions that would otherwise need enormous single launches.

pathway.milestone: orbital depots and deep-space propulsion such as nuclear thermal
pathway.unlocks: sustained lunar and Mars operations; nuclear thermal is still at the reactor-test stage.
